passage_text: Researchers studied the effect of a novel kinase inhibitor on the proliferation of human breast cancer cells (MCF‑7). Cells were treated with varying concentrations of the drug (0, 1, 5, 10, 20 µM) for 48 hours, after which cell viability was assessed using an MTT assay. The data were plotted as percent viability relative to untreated controls. The investigators also measured the phosphorylation status of downstream signaling proteins at each drug concentration to confirm target engagement. The study aimed to determine the IC₅₀ of the inhibitor and to assess whether a dose‑dependent reduction in viability correlated with decreased phosphorylation of the target kinase.
stem: Which drug concentration yields a cell viability closest to 50%?
explanation: The table shows that 5 µM results in 60% viability, which is the closest to 50% among the listed concentrations. 1 µM gives 85%, 10 µM gives 35%, and 20 µM gives 15%.
trap: Picking 10 µM because the IC₅₀ lies between 5 and 10 µM, without checking that 60% (5 µM) is 10 points from 50% while 35% (10 µM) is 15 points away.

stem: The investigators aim to test whether the loss of viability tracks inhibition of the target kinase. Which additional measurement across the same concentrations would best address this aim?

options.A: Phosphorylation of the target kinase at each concentration, compared with the viability values
options.B: Viability at one concentration only, measured at several time points
options.C: Viability of untreated cells at several time points
options.D: The IC50 of an unrelated drug in the same cells

explanation: Correct: A) The passage states the aim of correlating viability with phosphorylation of the target kinase, so measuring phosphorylation at each concentration is the direct test. Why the others are wrong: B) More viability measurements at one dose refine the time course but say nothing about the target. C) Untreated viability over time does not involve the drug or the kinase. D) An unrelated drug's IC50 does not show that this compound acts through the target.
trap: Choosing more viability measurements (B or C); they refine the viability curve but cannot show that the drug acts through the target kinase.

stem: Estimate the IC₅₀ (concentration that reduces viability by 50%) using linear interpolation between the 5 µM and 10 µM data points.
explanation: Between 5 µM (60%) and 10 µM (35%) the slope is (35 − 60)/(10 − 5) = −5% per µM. Dropping from 60% to 50% requires 10/5 = 2 µM, so IC50 ≈ 5 + 2 = 7.0 µM.
trap: Students may incorrectly use the slope from 10 µM to 20 µM, which would give a higher IC₅₀.

stem: Which of the following statements is NOT supported by Table 1?

options.A: Viability decreased at every increase in drug concentration.
options.B: At 20 µM, viability was 85 percentage points below that of untreated cells.
options.C: Between 1 µM and 5 µM, viability fell by 25 percentage points.
options.D: Phosphorylation of the target kinase fell as the concentration increased.

explanation: Correct: D is unsupported; Table 1 reports only viability and contains no phosphorylation data. Why the others are wrong: A) Viability falls 100, 85, 60, 35, 15%. B) 100 - 15 = 85 percentage points. C) 85 - 60 = 25 percentage points.
trap: Assuming that because phosphorylation was measured, a fall in phosphorylation is shown in the table.

stem: Which statement best describes the shape of the dose-response data in Table 1?

options.A: The decrease in viability per µM was smaller at higher concentrations than at lower ones.
options.B: Viability decreased by a constant amount for each µM added.
options.C: The 50% viability point lies between 10 µM and 20 µM.
options.D: Viability increased between 1 µM and 5 µM.

explanation: Correct: The decrease per µM is 15 (0 to 1 µM), 6.25 (1 to 5), 5 (5 to 10), and 2 (10 to 20) percentage points, so it shrinks at higher concentrations. Why the others are wrong: B) The per-µM change is not constant. C) Viability is already 35% at 10 µM, so the 50% point lies between 5 and 10 µM. D) Viability fell from 85% to 60% over that interval.
trap: Assuming a straight-line decline in viability, which a quick glance at the falling values might suggest.
